teile.einleitung: A scooter is a ride-on toy with a footboard, two or three small wheels and a handlebar. You stand on it with one foot and push off the ground with the other. In Switzerland it is called a “Trottinett”, from the French word “trottinette”; in Germany people say “Tretroller” or “Roller”.
wichtigste: You move an ordinary scooter forward by pushing off with your foot.
The folding scooter with small wheels was invented by the Swiss Wim Ouboter.
An e-scooter has an electric motor and a rechargeable battery.
In Switzerland an e-scooter may go no faster than 20 km/h.
On an e-scooter you must ride on the cycle lane or the road, not on the pavement.
A helmet protects your head when you ride a scooter.

abschnitte.text: A scooter consists of a **footboard**, two or three wheels and a handlebar. You usually brake with your foot on a metal guard over the back wheel or with a hand brake. Many scooters can be folded up and are easy to carry. For small children there are models with three wheels that do not tip over so easily.

Simple wooden scooters existed as children's toys more than a hundred years ago. At the end of the 1990s, the Swiss **Wim Ouboter** in Küsnacht on Lake Zurich developed a light folding aluminium scooter with small wheels. He wanted to cover short distances faster. His company **Micro** made the scooter popular again all over the world.

An **e-scooter** has an electric motor and a rechargeable battery, so you no longer have to push off. In Switzerland it counts as a light moped and may go no faster than **20 km/h**. From 14 to 16 you need a category M driving licence for it; from 16 you no longer do. In many towns you can hire e-scooters using an app.

On an ordinary scooter you count as a pedestrian and may ride on the pavement, but you must be considerate towards others. E-scooters, on the other hand, belong on the **cycle lane** or the road. A **helmet** and lights at dusk make you safer. Only one person should ever stand on a scooter.

With **stunt scooters**, teenagers do jumps and tricks in skateparks. These scooters are built especially sturdily and cannot be folded. There are even competitions in which the best riders show off somersaults and spins. For children the scooter is also a popular way to get to school.

begriffe.erklaerung: The board you stand on when riding a scooter.
A scooter with an electric motor and a rechargeable battery.
A battery that can be charged again.
An especially sturdy scooter for tricks in a skatepark.

gewusst: Wim Ouboter invented his scooter because the way to his favourite sausage stand was too far to walk and too short to drive.
The word “trottinette” comes from the French “trottiner”, which means something like to trot along with little steps.

teile.einleitung: Radio, also called broadcasting, transmits sounds such as music, news and radio plays using invisible radio waves. With a receiver you can listen to these programmes almost anywhere: at home, in the car or on the move. Radio was the first medium to reach people across a whole country live and at the same time.
wichtigste: Radio stations send sounds to the receiver using invisible radio waves.
From 1895, Guglielmo Marconi made radio transmission famous.
There have been regular radio broadcasts since the 1920s.
SRG is Switzerland's public broadcaster, with SRF, RTS, RSI and RTR.
Since the end of 2024, SRG programmes have been received via DAB+ instead of FM.
Households in Switzerland pay the media fee for it.
Radio can inform people, but it can also be misused for propaganda.

abschnitte.titel: How does the sound get into the radio?
abschnitte.text: In the studio, a microphone turns the sound into electrical signals. A transmitter sends these signals out as **radio waves** through an aerial. The waves travel at the speed of light and even pass through walls. The radio set picks them up with its aerial and turns them back into sound through a loudspeaker.

From 1895, the Italian **Guglielmo Marconi** transmitted signals without cables and became famous for it. In the 1920s, regular radio broadcasts began in many countries. In Switzerland, one of the first stations started in Lausanne in 1922, and in 1931 the Swiss Broadcasting Corporation **SRG** was founded. In Germany, the Nazi regime promoted the cheap “people's receiver” so that as many people as possible would hear its propaganda.

SRG is Switzerland's public broadcaster: **SRF** in German-speaking Switzerland, RTS in French-speaking Switzerland, RSI in Ticino and RTR for Romansh. Since the end of 2024, its programmes have no longer been broadcast on FM but digitally via **DAB+** and the internet. This is paid for mainly by the media fee, which all households pay, whether or not they have a set. In 2018 voters rejected the No Billag initiative to abolish the fees, with about 72 per cent voting no.

On the radio you can hear music, news, interviews, sports commentary and radio plays. The **weather forecast** and travel news about traffic jams are also part of it. Many programmes can now be listened to later as a podcast. In an emergency, the authorities also warn the population over the radio.

Media such as radio, television and newspapers are sometimes called the **fourth estate**, because they keep a check on those in power. In Switzerland, Article 17 of the Federal Constitution guarantees media freedom and forbids censorship. But not every news story is true, especially on social media. When you see a surprising report, check the source and see whether reliable media report the same thing.

begriffe.erklaerung: Invisible electromagnetic waves that carry signals through the air.
Digital radio with better sound and more stations.
The ultra-short-wave band, the usual way of receiving radio in the past.
Deliberate, one-sided influencing of the opinions of many people.

gewusst: In the Second World War many people in Germany secretly listened to the Swiss national station Beromünster to get reliable news.
Radio waves can travel round the Earth more than seven times in one second.
The first Swiss radio play was broadcast as early as the 1920s.

teile.einleitung: Swiss, whose full name is Swiss International Air Lines, is the largest airline in Switzerland. Its aeroplanes have a red Swiss cross on the tail and fly from Zurich and Geneva to many countries around the world. Swiss was founded in 2002 after the end of the famous Swissair.
wichtigste: There is a Swiss cross on the tail of Swiss aeroplanes.
Swiss was founded in 2002 after Swissair had to ground its planes in 2001.
The most important airport for Swiss is Zurich Airport.
Since 2007, Swiss has belonged to the German Lufthansa Group.
Swiss is a member of the Star Alliance, a group of airlines.
Swiss flies to destinations in Europe, America, Africa and Asia.

abschnitte.text: Swiss is Switzerland's **national airline**. Every year it carries many millions of passengers and also cargo. Its registered office is in Basel, and its most important **hub** is Zurich Airport. From there, large long-haul aircraft fly to places such as New York, Tokyo or Johannesburg.

Swissair, founded in 1931, was the well-known Swiss airline for about 70 years. In October 2001 it ran out of money and all its aircraft had to stay on the ground; this event is called the **grounding**. For many people in Switzerland it was a shock. The regional airline **Crossair** then became the new Swiss in 2002.

In 2005 the German airline **Lufthansa** bought Swiss, and since 2007 it has belonged entirely to the Lufthansa Group. However, Swiss still flies under its own name with the Swiss cross. It is a member of the **Star Alliance**, so travellers can easily change to flights of other partner airlines. The holiday airline Edelweiss also belongs to the same group.

Swiss flies Airbus and Boeing aircraft. For short routes it uses, among others, the **Airbus A220**, which it was one of the first airlines in the world to use. Large aircraft such as the Boeing 777 fly the long routes. The aircraft are looked after by pilots, cabin crew and engineers.

On flights, passengers often get a small piece of **Swiss chocolate**. Announcements are usually made in German, French and English. The red tail with the white cross is a well-known symbol at airports all over the world. Many aircraft are named after Swiss cantons or places.

begriffe.erklaerung: When an airline has to keep all its aircraft on the ground.
A large airport where many of an airline's flights start and passengers change planes.
A group of many airlines that work closely together.
All the aircraft of an airline together.

gewusst: Swiss was one of the first airlines in the world to use the Airbus A220, which was then still called the Bombardier CSeries.
With Swissair, Switzerland lost a company in 2001 that was seen as the country's flying calling card.

teile.einleitung: A robot is a machine that carries out tasks by itself and is controlled by a computer. Robots weld cars together, vacuum floors, operate alongside doctors and even drive across Mars. The word comes from Czech and originally means work.
wichtigste: A robot is a machine that carries out tasks by itself.
It is controlled by a computer and a program.
With sensors and cameras it senses its surroundings.
The word robot comes from the Czech word “robota” for work.
Especially many robot arms work in car factories.
At home, the robot vacuum cleaner cleans the floor.
Robot vehicles called rovers drive around on Mars.

abschnitte.text: A **robot** is a machine that is controlled by a computer and carries out tasks by itself. What it should do is written in a **program** that people have written. With **sensors** it measures things such as distance, light or touch, and with a camera it can see. Motors move its wheels, legs or gripping arms.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the word come from?
abschnitte.text: The word robot comes from Czech. The writer **Karel Čapek** used it in 1920 in his play “R.U.R.” for artificial workers. It comes from the word “robota”, which means work or forced labour. The science fiction author **Isaac Asimov** later wrote the famous three laws of robotics, according to which a robot must not harm people.

The first industrial robot, called Unimate, worked in a car factory in the USA from 1961. Today **robot arms** weld, paint and assemble in car factories almost without a break. They are strong and precise and never get tired. In warehouses, moving robots bring parcels to the staff.

Many families have a **robot vacuum cleaner** that moves through the flat by itself and cleans the floor. Robot lawnmowers are also common in Swiss gardens. In hospitals, surgical robots help surgeons with very delicate operations. At ETH Zurich, walking robots have been developed that, for example, inspect industrial plants.

Robots are especially useful where people cannot go. On Mars, robot vehicles called **rovers** drive around, for example Curiosity since 2012 and Perseverance since 2021. They photograph the landscape, examine rocks and look for traces of past life. Space probes are also basically robots that work by themselves far out in space.

begriffe.erklaerung: A component that measures something from the surroundings, such as light or distance.
A list of commands that tells a computer what to do.
A robot vehicle that drives around on another celestial body.
A robot arm that works in factories.

gewusst: The word robot is said to have actually been suggested by Karel Čapek's brother Josef.
The Mars rover Perseverance brought along a small helicopter called Ingenuity, the first aircraft to fly on another planet.
In some factories more robots work than people.

teile.einleitung: Wind energy is energy obtained from the power of the wind using large wind turbines. The wind turns the rotor blades, and a generator turns this into electricity. Because new wind keeps forming, wind energy is one of the renewable energies.
wichtigste: The wind turns the rotor blades of a wind turbine.
A generator in the nacelle turns the rotation into electricity.
Wind energy is renewable because new wind keeps forming.
According to Betz's law, a wind turbine can use at most about 59 per cent of the wind's energy.
Switzerland's largest wind farm is on Mont Crosin in the Bernese Jura.
In Switzerland, wind energy so far supplies only a small share of the electricity.
Countries such as Denmark and Germany obtain a great deal of electricity from wind.

abschnitte.titel: Where does the wind come from?
abschnitte.text: Wind forms because the Sun warms the Earth unevenly. Warm air rises and cooler air flows in to replace it, creating **differences in air pressure**. Because the Sun keeps shining, new wind keeps forming. That is why wind energy is a **renewable energy**. Unlike crude oil or natural gas, the wind never runs out.

A modern **wind turbine** consists of a tall tower, a nacelle and usually three long rotor blades. The wind turns the **rotor blades**, much as it turns a toy windmill. In the nacelle there is a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electricity. Large turbines are often more than 150 metres tall, and one rotor blade can be longer than a football pitch is wide. The nacelle turns into the wind automatically.

A wind turbine cannot take all the energy out of the wind, otherwise the air behind it would stand still. Around 1919, the German physicist Albert Betz calculated that at most about 59 per cent can be used. This is called **Betz's law**. In addition, the wind does not always blow with the same strength, so electricity production varies. In a storm, the turbines are switched off to protect them.

Switzerland's largest wind farm is on **Mont Crosin** in the Bernese Jura; the first turbines were built there in 1996. Another well-known wind farm has stood on the **Gotthard Pass** since 2020. Altogether only a few dozen large wind turbines turn in Switzerland so far. They currently supply less than one per cent of Switzerland's electricity. What makes them valuable is that they produce a lot of electricity in winter, when solar installations supply little.

Most of the world's wind turbines are in China, the USA and Germany. In Denmark, more than half the electricity comes from wind power. Many turbines stand at sea in **offshore wind farms**, where the wind blows more strongly and evenly. Critics complain that wind turbines change the landscape, make noise and can be dangerous for birds or bats. That is why every site is checked carefully.

begriffe.erklaerung: The turning part of the wind turbine with the rotor blades.
The housing at the top of the tower that holds the generator.
A group of several wind turbines in one place.
English for “off the coast”, that is, at sea.

gewusst: Centuries ago, windmills in Holland were already grinding grain and pumping water away.
The tips of large rotor blades can move at more than 300 kilometres per hour.
Sailing ships have also used wind energy for thousands of years.

teile.einleitung: A tram is an electric railway that runs on rails right through the streets of a town. In Germany it is called “Strassenbahn”; in Switzerland simply “Tram”. Trams carry lots of people through the city quietly and without exhaust fumes.
wichtigste: A tram gets its electricity from an overhead line.
Trams run on rails that are usually set into the road.
Zurich has the largest tram network in Switzerland.
Basel, Bern and Geneva also have tram networks.
The first trams were pulled by horses.
In 1881 the world's first electric tram ran in Berlin.
Basel trams run as far as Germany and France.

abschnitte.text: Above the tracks hangs an **overhead line**, a wire carrying electric current. On the roof of the tram, a **current collector**, also called a bow or pantograph, presses against this wire. The current drives electric motors that turn the wheels. The current flows back through the rails.

The first trams were pulled by **horses**; in Switzerland from 1862 in Geneva. In 1881 the world's first electric tram ran in Berlin-Lichterfelde, built by the company of **Werner von Siemens**. Around 1900 many Swiss towns got electric trams. Later, some towns replaced their trams with buses, but today many towns are building new tram lines again.

**Zurich** has the largest tram network in Switzerland, with many blue trams. Basel has green trams whose lines reach as far as Weil am Rhein in Germany and Saint-Louis in France. Bern and Geneva also have tram networks. New lines include, for example, the Glattalbahn near Zurich and the **Limmattalbahn**, which opened as far as Killwangen in 2022.

A long tram can carry more than 200 people at once. It runs quietly and produces no **exhaust fumes** in the city. Because it runs on its own tracks, it gets stuck in traffic less often than a car. Modern **low-floor trams** have no steps, so people in wheelchairs or with pushchairs can get on easily.

A tram has a much longer **braking distance** than a car and cannot swerve. That is why in Switzerland it usually has right of way. When crossing tram tracks, you should always look carefully both ways. Cyclists should cross the rails as close to a right angle as possible so that the wheel does not get stuck in the groove.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wire carrying electric current above the tracks.
A bow on the roof that takes the current from the overhead line.
A tram with a low floor and no steps at the entrance.
The distance a vehicle needs before it comes to a stop.

gewusst: If a bus leaves every 12 minutes and a tram every 18 minutes, and both start at 8.00, they leave at the same time again at 8.36.
Zurich's Cobra tram was developed and built in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The internet is a huge network that connects computers, mobile phones and other devices all over the world. Through the internet we send messages, watch videos, look for information and play together. It has changed our lives as much as printing once did.
wichtigste: The internet connects computers all over the world.
It grew out of ARPANET, which went into operation in the USA in 1969.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the World Wide Web at CERN near Geneva.
Swiss websites often end in “.ch”, which stands for Confoederatio Helvetica.
You never share personal data such as your address and phone number with strangers.
You may only put photos of other people on the internet with their permission.
If something on the internet frightens you, tell an adult you trust.

abschnitte.text: The internet is a network of many millions of computers and networks connected by cables, radio and satellites. So that all devices understand each other, they use shared rules called **protocols**. Data are split into small packets, sent off and put back together at their destination. Every device on the network has its own number, the **IP address**.

The internet grew out of **ARPANET**, a research network in the USA that connected the first computers in 1969. In the 1980s it grew into a worldwide network of universities. From 1989, Tim Berners-Lee developed the World Wide Web with its linked web pages at CERN near Geneva. After that, from the 1990s, the internet also became popular in homes.

The country ending **.ch** stands for Confoederatio Helvetica, the Latin name of Switzerland. Geneva is home to the International Telecommunication Union ITU, which sets worldwide rules for telecommunications and the internet. Some cantons are also trying out **e-voting**, that is, casting your vote electronically over the internet. Comparison websites also help you compare the prices of different suppliers before buying something.

Never share your address, phone number or passwords with strangers. You may only put photos of other people on the internet if they agree. If you see something that frightens you, tell an adult you trust. Before buying online, check the seller and the reviews so that you do not fall for a **scam**.

The internet makes knowledge available to a great many people, much as printing once did. In some countries, however, there is **censorship**, which means the state controls or bans what may appear on the internet. In Switzerland, freedom of opinion and of the media is protected by the Federal Constitution. Even so, the same applies on the internet: insulting others and telling lies about them is forbidden.

begriffe.erklaerung: A fixed rule for how computers exchange data with each other.
A number by which every device on the internet is recognised.
When the state controls or bans what may be published.
Voting in a ballot or election over the internet.

gewusst: Under the oceans lie hundreds of thick undersea cables that carry almost all data traffic between the continents.
The internet and the World Wide Web are not the same thing, because the Web is only one service on the internet, like e-mail.
Today about two thirds of all people in the world use the internet (as of 2024).

teile.einleitung: A smartphone is a mobile phone that is also a small computer. You usually operate it with your finger on a touchscreen and can use it to make calls, take photos, surf the internet and use apps. Since the first iPhone in 2007, the smartphone has changed the everyday lives of billions of people.
wichtigste: A smartphone is a mobile phone with the abilities of a computer.
You usually operate it with your finger on the touchscreen.
The iPhone brought the big breakthrough for smartphones in 2007.
Most smartphones run on Android or iOS.
Sensors detect, for example, whether the device is held upright or sideways.
With the Swiss app TWINT you can pay without cash using your smartphone.
A hundred years ago there were no smartphones.

abschnitte.text: A **smartphone** combines a telephone, camera, music player, satnav and computer in one device. It is operated via a **touchscreen**, which recognises touches of the finger. Extra programs, the **apps**, are downloaded from an app store. With them the smartphone becomes an alarm clock, dictionary, games device or timetable.

The first mobile phones with computer functions already existed in the 1990s, but they had keys or a stylus. The big breakthrough came in 2007 with Apple's **iPhone**, which was operated only with your fingers. A year later the first smartphones with Google's **Android** operating system came onto the market. Today almost all young people in Switzerland have their own smartphone.

Inside, a small but very powerful processor does the work. An **accelerometer** detects whether the device is held upright or sideways and turns the picture to match. Other sensors measure light, nearness and direction, and a satellite receiver works out the location. A rechargeable battery supplies the power and has to be charged regularly.

**TWINT** is a Swiss app that lets you pay without cash using your smartphone. You use it in shops, in online shops or to send money to friends. The app has been widespread in its present form since 2017 and is used by millions of people in Switzerland. To pay, you need a bank account, so with children a parent usually helps.

Smartphones need rare **raw materials**, which are often mined under difficult conditions. That is why it is worth using a device for a long time and handing in old phones so that the raw materials can be recycled. Too much screen time can disturb your sleep and distract you from other things. That is why many families agree on phone rules together, for example no smartphone in the bedroom.

begriffe.erklaerung: A screen that reacts to touch.
A program that you load onto the smartphone.
The basic software that controls the device, such as Android or iOS.
A battery that can be charged again.

gewusst: A smartphone today is much more powerful than the computers that controlled the Moon landing in 1969.
The German word “Handy” for a mobile phone only looks English, because in English people say “mobile phone” or “cell phone”.
A smartphone contains dozens of different chemical elements, including gold.

teile.einleitung: A tractor is a powerful vehicle used mainly in farming. It pulls ploughs, trailers and many other machines across fields and meadows. In Switzerland people say “Traktor”; in Germany it is often called “Schlepper” or “Trecker”.
wichtigste: A tractor is used mainly in farming.
Tractors have large rear wheels with deep tread so that they do not spin on soft ground.
Many different machines can be attached to a tractor.
Using the power take-off, the tractor can also drive machines.
In Switzerland you may drive a tractor from the age of 14 with a category G licence.
The first tractors were powered by steam.

abschnitte.text: A tractor is a **towing vehicle**, a vehicle built mainly to pull and push. It is not fast, but it is very strong. The large rear wheels with deep **tread** grip the ground well. Many tractors today have four-wheel drive.

At the back and front, a tractor has **hydraulics** that can raise and lower machines such as a plough, harrow or mower. Using the **power take-off**, a turning shaft at the back, the tractor drives, for example, a hay baler or a loader wagon. With a front loader it can lift soil or manure like a small digger. In this way one tractor replaces many working animals and people.

In the past, horses and oxen pulled the plough. In the 19th century there were the first heavy **steam tractors**. Around 1890 the first tractors with petrol engines appeared in the USA. In Switzerland, the company **Hürlimann** in Wil SG built tractors from 1929; Bührer and Vevey were also well-known makers.

There are many tractors on Swiss farms because even steep meadows are farmed. For very steep ground there are special vehicles with a low centre of gravity, called **transporters**, and two-axle mowers. Young people may drive farm vehicles up to 30 km/h from the age of **14** with a category G licence. To get it, they attend a course and take a test.

Today's tractors have comfortable cabs with screens and air conditioning. With the help of **GPS**, they can drive exactly straight across a field almost by themselves. Large tractors have several hundred horsepower. Tractors powered by electricity or biogas are also being developed.

begriffe.erklaerung: A turning shaft on a tractor that drives attached machines.
A technology that lifts heavy things using oil under pressure.
A tool that breaks up the soil and turns it over.
A driving licence for farm vehicles from the age of 14.

gewusst: Some large tractor tyres are taller than an adult.
In tractor pulling competitions, modified tractors pull heavy sledges as far as they can.

teile.einleitung: A nuclear power station is a power station that produces electricity from the energy of atomic nuclei. Heavy atomic nuclei, usually of uranium, are split. Nuclear power stations supply a lot of electricity but are also controversial.
wichtigste: Nuclear power stations produce electricity by splitting heavy atomic nuclei.
The fuel is usually uranium.
Nuclear fission releases heat, which turns water into steam and drives turbines.
Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station, Beznau, went into operation in 1969.
The Mühleberg nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down for good in 2019.
Today Beznau 1 and 2, Gösgen and Leibstadt are still running in Switzerland.
The Chernobyl reactor accident in 1986 showed how dangerous an accident can be.

abschnitte.text: In the **reactor**, heavy atomic nuclei, usually of **uranium**, are hit with neutrons and split. This **nuclear fission** produces large amounts of heat and more neutrons. These split new nuclei in turn, creating a controlled **chain reaction**. The heat turns water into steam, which turns a turbine. Finally, a generator turns this into electric current.

Switzerland's first commercial nuclear power station was **Beznau** in the canton of Aargau; it went into operation in 1969. Later came **Gösgen** in the canton of Solothurn and **Leibstadt** in Aargau; Leibstadt is the largest. The **Mühleberg** nuclear power station in the canton of Bern was shut down for good at the end of 2019 and is now being dismantled. Together, Switzerland's nuclear power stations supply about a third of the country's own electricity. Their safety is supervised by the Swiss Federal Nuclear Safety Inspectorate ENSI.

In a serious accident, **radioactivity** can escape and harm people and nature. In 1986 a reactor exploded at **Chernobyl** in what is now Ukraine; the surrounding area is still closed off today. In 2011 an earthquake and a tsunami damaged the Fukushima nuclear power station in Japan. In Switzerland too, in 1969, there was an accident in the small experimental reactor in a rock cavern near **Lucens** in the canton of Vaud. That is why very strict safety rules apply to nuclear power stations.

abschnitte.titel: What to do with the waste?
abschnitte.text: Spent fuel rods remain dangerously radioactive for a very long time, in some cases for hundreds of thousands of years. They are first kept in interim stores, for example the **Würenlingen interim store**. In the long term they are to be sealed deep in the rock in a **deep geological repository**. In 2022 the organisation responsible, Nagra, proposed the Nördlich Lägern area for this. It will be many years before such a repository is built.

Nuclear power stations supply a lot of electricity day and night and give off hardly any **carbon dioxide** while doing so. On the other hand, there is the risk of serious accidents and the unsolved problem of radioactive waste. In 2017 Swiss voters approved the **Energy Strategy 2050**, which bans the building of new nuclear power stations. The existing plants may keep running as long as they are safe. Whether new nuclear power stations should be allowed again is being debated in politics once more.

begriffe.erklaerung: The splitting of a heavy atomic nucleus, which releases a lot of energy.
A heavy, slightly radioactive metal used as fuel in nuclear power stations.
A process in which each splitting sets off further splittings.
Invisible radiation from decaying atomic nuclei that can harm living things.
A tall tower in which water is cooled, recognisable by its white cloud of steam.

gewusst: The white cloud above the cooling tower of a nuclear power station is harmless water vapour.
A single small uranium fuel pellet supplies about as much energy as roughly a tonne of hard coal.
At 144 metres, the cooling tower at Leibstadt is one of the tallest structures in Switzerland.

teile.einleitung: The World Wide Web, www or the Web for short, is a system of billions of web pages connected to each other by links. It was invented by the British computer scientist Tim Berners-Lee from 1989 at CERN near Geneva. The Web is not the same as the internet; it is one of its most important services.
wichtigste: The abbreviation “www” stands for World Wide Web.
Tim Berners-Lee invented the Web in 1989 at CERN near Geneva.
Web pages are connected to each other by links, also called hyperlinks.
On 30 April 1993, CERN released the Web for everyone to use freely.
You look at web pages with a program called a browser.
The Web is a service on the internet, like e-mail.
Today there are more than a billion websites worldwide.

abschnitte.text: The **World Wide Web** consists of web pages containing texts, pictures and videos. If you click on a **link**, you jump to another page, no matter which computer in the world it is stored on. With a **browser** such as Firefox, Chrome or Safari you can look at these pages. Every page has its own address, the URL, for example with www at the beginning.

**CERN** is a large research centre for particle physics near Geneva on the border with France. Thousands of researchers from many countries worked there and wanted to share their information. So in March 1989 the Briton **Tim Berners-Lee** proposed a system of linked documents. In 1990 he built the first web server and the first browser on a NeXT computer.

Berners-Lee invented three important building blocks: **HTML** is the language in which web pages are written. HTTP is the rule for how browsers and servers exchange pages. The URL is the address where a page can be found. These building blocks are still used today, in further developed form, on every website.

On 30 April 1993, CERN released the technology of the Web for **free use**. Nobody had to pay fees for it, and everyone was allowed to build their own web pages. This was an important reason why the Web spread so quickly all over the world. From the mid-1990s, more and more companies, newspapers and private individuals went online.

Today billions of people use the Web for learning, shopping, playing and communicating. Online encyclopedias, video platforms and social networks are part of the Web. In 1994 Tim Berners-Lee founded the **W3C**, which still sets shared rules for the Web today. The very first website can still be visited at CERN at its old address.

begriffe.erklaerung: A single page on the World Wide Web that you can look at.
A clickable reference that takes you to another page.
A program for displaying web pages.
The language in which web pages are written.
The address of a web page.

gewusst: Tim Berners-Lee's boss wrote the words “vague but exciting” on the first proposal.
On the first web server there was a note saying that the computer must not be switched off.
The very first photo on the Web showed a band made up of CERN staff members.

teile.einleitung: A computer is a machine that processes data with the help of programs. It can calculate, write, show pictures, play music and much more. Today computers are found not only in laptops but also in smartphones, cars and washing machines.
wichtigste: A computer processes data according to the commands of a program.
Inside, a computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1.
In 1941 Konrad Zuse built the first working programmable computer.
The first computers were as big as a room.
Today there is also a small computer inside a smartphone.
The Swiss Niklaus Wirth developed the programming language Pascal at ETH Zurich.
To keep your computer safe, you should never tell anyone your password.

abschnitte.text: The word computer comes from the English “to compute”, which means to calculate. A computer works on the principle of **input, processing, output**. You enter something, the computer processes it and shows a result. The commands telling it what to do are in a **program**. Without programs, a computer would just be a box of metal and plastic.

Inside, a computer calculates only with the two digits 0 and 1, the so-called **binary system**. You can imagine it like a light switch that is either off or on. A single 0 or 1 is called a **bit**; eight bits together make a byte. With many millions of such switches, a computer can represent numbers, letters, pictures and sounds.

The computer's brain is the **processor**; it carries out the commands. The working memory holds data that are needed right now. Files are stored permanently on the hard disk or an SSD. You type letters with the **keyboard**, and you move the pointer on the screen with the mouse. The well-known Swiss company Logitech, founded in the canton of Vaud, makes such mice and keyboards.

In 1941 the German engineer **Konrad Zuse** built the Z3 in Berlin, the first working programmable computer. The first computers were as big as a room and weighed several tonnes. A later machine by Zuse, the Z4, was used at ETH Zurich from 1950. Thanks to small electronic components, transistors and microchips, computers became smaller and faster. From the 1980s, home computers moved into many living rooms.

The Swiss computer scientist **Niklaus Wirth** developed the programming language **Pascal** at ETH Zurich around 1970. Many people all over the world learned to program with it. For his work, Wirth received the Turing Award in 1984, a kind of Nobel Prize for computer science. Not far away, at CERN near Geneva, the World Wide Web was invented in 1989.

In 1997 the computer **Deep Blue** beat the world chess champion Garry Kasparov in a match. In March 2016 the program AlphaGo by DeepMind won 4 to 1 against the Go professional Lee Sedol. Programs like these show what **artificial intelligence** can do. Safety is also important, though: you should never tell anyone your password. You should also only install programs from safe sources.

begriffe.erklaerung: The part of a computer that carries out commands and calculates.
A list of commands that tells the computer what to do.
The smallest unit of information, a 0 or a 1.
A number system that works only with the digits 0 and 1.
A secret word that protects a computer or an account.

gewusst: A smartphone today is much more powerful than the computers used to fly the first people to the Moon in 1969.
The American computer ENIAC from 1946 weighed about 27 tonnes.
The word “bug” for a computer fault became famous when a real moth was found in a computer in 1947.

teile.einleitung: The Grande Dixence is a huge dam in the canton of Valais that holds back the reservoir Lac des Dix. At 285 metres, it is the highest gravity dam in the world. Its water is turned into electricity in power stations for the whole of Switzerland.
wichtigste: The Grande Dixence dam is in the canton of Valais.
It is 285 metres high, making it the highest gravity dam in the world.
It was built from 1951 to 1961.
The lake it holds back is called Lac des Dix.
Most of the water comes from glaciers and is brought in through long tunnels.
The plant supplies valuable electricity, especially in winter.
The dam contains about six million cubic metres of concrete.

abschnitte.text: The Grande Dixence lies high up in the **Val des Dix**, a side valley of the Val d'Hérens in the canton of **Valais**. It belongs to the municipality of Hérémence south of Sion. The top of the dam is at about 2365 metres above sea level. Behind it, the reservoir **Lac des Dix** stretches for several kilometres. All around rise high Valais mountains and glaciers.

The Grande Dixence is 285 metres high, more than twice as tall as the Prime Tower in Zurich. It is a **gravity dam**, which holds back the water by its enormous weight alone. At the bottom it is almost 200 metres thick; at the top only about 15 metres. The crest is about 750 metres long. Inside, there are inspection galleries in which experts monitor the dam.

Today's dam was built from 1951 to 1961 and replaced a smaller, older dam. Thousands of workers worked at great height, often in cold and snow. Altogether about six million cubic metres of **concrete** were used. It is often said that this would be enough to build a wall round the Earth. The Grande Dixence is still regarded as a masterpiece of Swiss **civil engineering** today.

The Lac des Dix can store about 400 million cubic metres of water. Most of the water comes from the meltwater of dozens of **glaciers**, including from the area around Zermatt. Pumping stations and about 100 kilometres of **tunnels** carry it to the lake. From there it flows down through penstocks into the Rhône valley to power stations such as Bieudron and Fionnay. Because the water is collected in summer and used in winter, the plant supplies important **winter electricity**.

In summer, buses go up to the foot of the dam. By cable car or on foot you can reach the crest and the lake. On guided tours you can also visit the inside of the dam. Popular hiking trails lead around the Lac des Dix, for example to the Cabane des Dix. The Grande Dixence is one of the best-known sights in Valais.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wall that blocks a valley and holds back water to form a lake.
A dam that holds back the water by its great weight alone.
An artificial lake behind a dam.
An underground passage through which water is channelled.

gewusst: The Grande Dixence is higher than any building in Switzerland.
The Bieudron power station uses a drop of almost 1900 metres; when it opened, that was a world record.
So that the water from Zermatt can reach the Lac des Dix, some of it is pumped up the mountain.

teile.einleitung: The wheel is a round disc that turns around an axle, and it is one of the most important inventions of humankind. It was invented about 5500 years ago and made it much easier to move heavy loads. Without wheels there would be no bicycles, cars or trains, and no clocks with cogwheels either.
wichtigste: A wheel turns around an axle in its centre.
The wheel was invented about 5500 years ago.
The first wheels were made of wood.
Early wheels were heavy discs without spokes.
Later, lighter spoked wheels appeared.
Very old wooden wheels have also been found in lake-dwelling settlements in Switzerland.
Wheels are found not only in vehicles but also in machines and clocks.

abschnitte.text: A **wheel** is a round object that turns around an **axle**. Because the wheel rolls instead of scraping along the ground, you need much less force to move a load. The wheel and axle together are one of the simple machines in physics. Cogwheels, pulleys and flywheels are also based on this idea.

The wheel was invented about 5500 years ago, that is, around 3500 BC. The oldest finds come from Mesopotamia, Eastern Europe and the Alpine region. Potters probably used turning discs early on, the **potter's wheel**. Soon afterwards, people built carts and wagons pulled by cattle.

The first wheels were made of wood and were heavy **disc wheels** made of one or more planks. In lake-dwelling settlements on Lake Zurich and in Slovenia, archaeologists found wooden wheels about 5000 years old. They survived in the damp lake bed because hardly any air could get to them. Finds like these show that the wheel spread quickly across Europe.

Around 2000 BC, lighter **spoked wheels** appeared. With them, fast chariots and travelling carts could be built. Later, wooden wheels were protected with iron tyres, and in the 19th century air-filled rubber tyres were added. These still make bicycles and cars quieter and more comfortable today.

Today we come across wheels everywhere: on bicycles, cars, trains, pushchairs and wheeled suitcases. In machines, **cogwheels** pass on forces, for example in gearboxes or in mechanical Swiss watches. Wind turbines and water wheels use the power of nature. Even a Ferris wheel at the fair is basically a giant wheel.

begriffe.erklaerung: The rod around which a wheel turns.
A rod that connects the centre of a wheel to its rim.
A wheel with teeth that can drive other wheels.
Houses on stilts on lake shores from the Stone and Bronze Ages.

gewusst: The peoples of ancient America knew the wheel in toys but did not use it for carts.
A bicycle has spoked wheels, which are very light and yet strong.
One of the oldest wooden wheels in the world was found in Ljubljana in Slovenia.

teile.einleitung: A 3D printer is a machine that makes real objects you can hold. It builds them up layer by layer out of plastic, metal or other materials. In this way it makes toy figures, spare parts and even parts for medicine.
wichtigste: A 3D printer builds objects up layer by layer.
As a template, it needs a three-dimensional computer model.
In home 3D printers, the plastic is fed in as a thread from a reel.
A nozzle melts the plastic thread and lays it down in thin lines.
The first 3D printers were developed in the 1980s.
Experts call the process additive manufacturing.
3D printers are used in industry, medicine, schools and at home.

abschnitte.text: An ordinary printer puts ink onto a flat sheet of paper. A 3D printer, on the other hand, creates objects with length, width and height. It only adds material where it is needed. That is why it is called **additive manufacturing**, because additive means adding. When milling or carving, by contrast, material is taken away.

It starts with a **3D model**, which you draw on a computer or create with a 3D scanner. A special program, the **slicer**, cuts the model into many thin slices. For each slice it works out the exact path of the nozzle. The computer then sends these commands to the printer.

Most home printers use **fused deposition modelling**. A plastic thread, the **filament**, is unwound from a reel and heated to about 200 degrees in a hot nozzle. The nozzle moves back and forth and lays the soft plastic down in fine lines, which quickly harden again. When one layer is finished, it carries on one step higher. With layers of 0.2 millimetres, an object 3 centimetres tall therefore needs 150 layers.

There are also 3D printers that work with liquid resin. A beam of light hardens the resin layer by layer; this is called **stereolithography**. The American Chuck Hull patented this method in the 1980s. Other machines melt fine metal powder together with a **laser**; this is how parts for aircraft are made, for example.

In medicine, made-to-measure **prostheses**, dental splints and models of organs for planning operations are printed. Companies use them to build samples of new products quickly, called prototypes. If you have a broken plastic part, you can sometimes print a spare part yourself. In several countries, small houses have even been built with giant concrete printers.

Many Swiss schools, libraries and so-called makerspaces have their own 3D printers. There, children and teenagers can design and print their own ideas. Universities such as **ETH Zurich** also research new printing methods, for example for concrete buildings. In this way you learn technology, maths and design at the same time.

begriffe.erklaerung: A plastic thread on a reel that a home 3D printer prints with.
A computer program that splits a 3D model into many thin layers.
Making things by adding material layer by layer.
The first sample of a new product, made for testing.

gewusst: A 3D printer has already been tested on the International Space Station ISS so that astronauts can make tools themselves.
A larger object can take many hours or even days in a 3D printer.
A commonly used plastic is PLA, which is made from plants such as maize.

teile.einleitung: Saving energy means using less energy without going without important things. Saving energy protects the environment and your wallet. Even small everyday habits can make a big difference.
wichtigste: Saving energy means using electricity, heat and fuel carefully and wisely.
The cleanest energy is the energy you never use in the first place.
When cooking, a lid on the pan saves a lot of energy.
In winter the most economical way to air a room is briefly, with the window wide open.
LED lamps use much less electricity than old light bulbs.
When buying, the energy label shows how economical an appliance is.
Well-insulated houses need much less energy for heating.

abschnitte.text: A large part of the world's energy still comes from crude oil, natural gas and coal. Burning them produces **carbon dioxide**, which makes climate change worse. Renewable energy also needs space, materials and money for power stations. So using less protects the **climate** and saves money. In winter 2022/23 the federal government called on the population to save energy because an **energy shortage** was threatening.

Heating uses the most energy in Swiss households. Just one degree less room temperature saves a few per cent of heating energy. In winter it is best to air a room briefly with the window wide open; this is called **shock ventilation**. Windows left tilted open, on the other hand, let heat escape for hours. Taking a shower instead of a bath saves hot water and so also saves energy.

A lid on the pan makes the water boil faster and saves a lot of energy. Appliances on **standby** secretly use electricity even when switched off; a power strip with a switch helps against this. **LED lamps** use only a fraction of the electricity of an old light bulb and last much longer. When buying, the coloured **energy label** shows whether a fridge or washing machine is economical. Class A is the best.

Short journeys on foot or by bike use almost no energy and keep you fit. Trains, trams and buses use much less energy per person than a car. Switzerland has one of the densest **public transport networks** in the world. Air travel also uses a great deal of energy per person. So if you go on holiday closer to home, you save energy.

Good **insulation** in walls, roof and windows keeps the heat in the house like a thick winter coat. Since 1998 Switzerland has had the **Minergie** building standard for especially economical houses. Heat pumps take heat from the air or the ground and need little electricity to do so. The federal programme SwissEnergy gives tips on saving. Many municipalities support renovations with money.

begriffe.erklaerung: A ready mode in which an appliance seems to be off but still uses electricity.
Airing a room for a few minutes with the window wide open.
A layer on house walls and roofs that keeps heat inside the house.
A coloured label that shows how much energy an appliance uses.

gewusst: One LED lamp can shine as long as many old light bulbs one after the other.
A fridge standing next to the oven has to work harder and uses more electricity.
Heating water takes much more energy than you might think, so short showers save a lot.

teile.einleitung: A bicycle is a vehicle with two wheels that you power with your muscles. In Germany it is called “Fahrrad”; in Switzerland “Velo”. It is quiet, healthy, environmentally friendly and one of the most important means of transport in the world.
wichtigste: You power a bicycle with your muscles.
The chain connects the pedals to the back wheel.
Karl Drais's running machine from 1817 did not yet have pedals.
A dynamo turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights.
Friction slowly brings a rolling bicycle to a stop.
In Switzerland many children take a cycling test at school.
The tread on the tyre helps it grip better.

abschnitte.text: A bicycle has a **frame**, two wheels with tyres, handlebars, a saddle and pedals. When you push the pedals, the chainring at the front turns, and the **chain** passes the force on to the back wheel. With the **gears** you can ride uphill more easily or go faster on the flat. A little oil on the chain reduces friction.

In 1817, **Karl Drais** in Mannheim invented the running machine, also called the draisine. It did not yet have pedals; you pushed yourself along with your feet. Later came the **penny-farthing** with its huge front wheel and, around 1885, the safety bicycle with chain drive, which looks like our bicycles today. In 1888, John Boyd Dunlop's air-filled tyre made riding much more comfortable.

In Switzerland a roadworthy bicycle needs two brakes, a bell, lights at the front and back, and reflectors. A **dynamo** turns the movement of the wheel into electricity for the lights; today there are also battery lights. When you stop pedalling, **friction** and air resistance slowly bring the bicycle to a stop. If you ride at 15 kilometres per hour, you travel 30 kilometres in two hours.

In Switzerland there are thousands of kilometres of **cycle paths** and signposted cycle routes from “Veloland Schweiz”. Children up to 12 may ride on the pavement if there is no cycle lane, and they must be considerate towards pedestrians. Many schools have a **cycling test**. A cycle helmet is not compulsory but is strongly recommended.

Cycle races such as the **Tour de France** or the Tour de Suisse, which has existed since 1933, are very popular. There are racing bikes, mountain bikes, BMX bikes and **e-bikes** with electric motors. When you cycle, you get exercise and produce no exhaust fumes. That is why the bicycle is good for your health and for the environment.

begriffe.erklaerung: The first two-wheeler, by Karl Drais, without pedals.
A small generator that makes electricity from movement.
A device that lets you pedal more easily or with more effort.
A force that slows down a movement.

gewusst: It is estimated that there are more than twice as many bicycles as cars in the world.
On a penny-farthing the front wheel was often more than 1.5 metres tall, so that each turn of the pedals took you a long way.

teile.einleitung: A ship is a large watercraft that carries people and goods across seas, lakes and rivers. People were already building ships out of wood thousands of years ago; today the largest are made of steel and are longer than three football pitches. Even though they are so heavy, they do not sink.
wichtigste: A steel ship floats because it pushes aside a lot of water and buoyancy holds it up.
Large cargo ships travel up the Rhine as far as Basel.
In the past, the wind drove the explorers' ships.
Columbus set off in 1492 with three ships; the largest was the Santa María.
From 1519 to 1522, Magellan's expedition was the first to sail all the way around the world.
Today, container ships carry most of the world's goods.
Switzerland also has ocean-going ships; their home port is Basel.

abschnitte.text: A ship's hull pushes water aside; we say it **displaces** water. The water pushes back from below, and this force is called **buoyancy**. If the displaced water weighs as much as the whole ship, the ship floats. The Greek scholar Archimedes discovered this more than 2000 years ago.

The front part is called the **bow**, the back part the **stern**. Looking forward, the left side is **port** and the right side is starboard. The rudder is used for steering, and a propeller under the water drives modern ships. The ship is steered from the bridge, where the captain is in command.

For a long time, the **wind** drove ships across the seas. In 1492, Christopher **Columbus** set off with three ships, the Santa María, the Pinta and the Niña, and first stopped in the Canary Islands. He then crossed the Atlantic and reached America. From 1519 to 1522, Ferdinand **Magellan**'s expedition was the first to sail all the way around the Earth.

There are **container ships**, tankers for crude oil, ferries for cars, cruise ships for holidays and fishing boats. The largest container ships are about 400 metres long and carry more than 20,000 containers. Icebreakers can break through thick ice. Warships and submarines belong to a country's navy.

Although Switzerland has no coast, large cargo ships travel up the **Rhine** as far as **Basel**. In the Rhine ports, containers, grain and fuel are unloaded and reloaded. Since 1941 there has been a Swiss ocean-going fleet whose ships are registered in Basel. Many passenger boats also take people on trips on the Swiss lakes.

begriffe.erklaerung: The force of water that pushes floating things upwards.
The front part of a ship.
The back part of a ship.
The left side of a ship when you look forward.
A large metal box of standard size for goods.

gewusst: Because they can travel through the desert for weeks, camels are also called “ships of the desert”.
In 1912 the Titanic was thought to be unsinkable, yet it sank on its first voyage after hitting an iceberg.

teile.einleitung: Responsive web design means that a website automatically adapts to the size of the screen. The same page then looks good on a mobile phone, a tablet and a big monitor. Today almost all modern websites are built this way.
wichtigste: With responsive web design, the page adapts to the screen size.
With media queries in CSS, you react to different screen widths.
Mobile first means designing for small screens first.
The viewport meta element in the head section is important for mobile phones.
The CSS unit vw depends on the width of the browser window.
CSS Grid and Flexbox are layout systems for flexible arrangements.
The width at which a layout changes is called a breakpoint.

abschnitte.text: In the past, websites were mostly designed for a fixed computer screen. With the success of smartphones from 2007 this became a problem, because you saw tiny writing on your phone. With **responsive web design**, the page reacts to the available width. The term was coined by the web designer Ethan Marcotte in 2010.

With **media queries**, you write rules in CSS that only apply from a certain screen width. The width at which the layout changes is called a **breakpoint**. An example: on a mobile phone, three boxes are shown one below the other, and from a width of 768 pixels side by side. This keeps the page easy to read everywhere.

In responsive layouts, widths are often given in **percent** so that elements adapt to the available space. The unit vw stands for one hundredth of the width of the browser window. Pictures are often given the rule never to become wider than their container. The **viewport** meta element in the head section tells the mobile phone not simply to show the page shrunk down.

**Flexbox** arranges elements flexibly in a row or column and shares out the space automatically. **CSS Grid** divides the page like a grid into rows and columns. Both techniques make it much easier to build layouts for different screens. They are supported by all common browsers today.

With the **mobile first** approach, you design the version for small screens first. There you have to limit yourself to the essentials, which makes the page clearer. For bigger screens you then add more columns and elements. Because many people today mainly browse on their phones, this approach is widespread.

begriffe.erklaerung: A language used to set the appearance of websites.
A CSS rule that only applies at certain screen sizes.
The screen width at which a layout changes.
The visible area of a website in the browser window.
The arrangement of texts, pictures and elements on a page.

gewusst: Search engines rate websites better if they also work well on mobile phones.
In a browser's developer tools you can test how a page looks on different mobile phones.

teile.einleitung: A battery is an energy store that turns chemical energy into electric current. It supplies electricity for torches, remote controls, clocks and toys without any plug socket. A rechargeable battery is found in every mobile phone and every electric car.
wichtigste: A battery turns stored chemical energy into electric current.
Around 1800, Alessandro Volta built the first usable battery, the voltaic pile.
A battery that can be recharged is called a rechargeable battery or accumulator.
Batteries supply direct current, which always flows in the same direction.
A lamp only lights up when the circuit is closed.
Empty batteries go back into the collection box in the shop.
The unit volt is named after Alessandro Volta.

abschnitte.text: A **battery** has two terminals, a positive one and a negative one. Inside, chemical reactions take place that release electrons at one terminal. If you connect the two terminals with a wire and a device, the electrons flow and an electric current is produced. When the supply of chemicals is used up, the battery is flat.

For a simple **circuit** you need at least a battery, wires and something that uses the current, such as a lamp. The lamp only lights up when the circuit is closed and the current can flow all the way round. A switch opens or closes the circuit. Batteries supply **direct current**, which always flows in the same direction, whereas the current from a plug socket is alternating current and regularly changes direction.

Around 1800, the Italian **Alessandro Volta** stacked discs of zinc and copper on top of each other in turn and put cardboard soaked in salt water between them. This **voltaic pile** was the first usable battery that supplied current continuously. Volta was inspired by experiments with frogs' legs by his fellow Italian Luigi Galvani. The unit of electrical voltage, the volt, is named after Volta.

A battery that can be charged again is called a **rechargeable battery** or accumulator. Mobile phones, laptops, e-bikes and electric cars usually contain lithium-ion batteries. They are light and store a lot of energy. In 2019 three researchers received the Nobel Prize in Chemistry for developing them.

Batteries contain metals that are valuable but in some cases also poisonous. In Switzerland you are required to hand back empty batteries, and every shop that sells batteries must take them back. There are **collection boxes** there; handing them in is free because a fee has already been paid when you buy them. Damaged lithium batteries can catch fire and so must never go in the rubbish bag.

begriffe.erklaerung: The connection of a battery, positive or negative.
A closed path through which electric current flows.
A battery that can be charged again.
The unit of electrical voltage.

gewusst: Some animals also produce electricity: the electric eel can give off shocks of several hundred volts.
A bicycle dynamo also makes electricity, but from the movement of the wheel instead of from chemistry.
With a lemon, a piece of copper and a galvanised nail you can make a small battery.

teile.einleitung: A telephone is a device that lets people talk to each other over long distances. It turns the voice into electrical signals or radio waves and, at the other end, back into sound. In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received the patent for the telephone; today almost everyone carries a mobile phone in their pocket.
wichtigste: With a telephone you can talk over great distances.
In 1876 Alexander Graham Bell received a patent for the telephone.
In the past, all telephones were connected to the telephone network by cable.
A mobile phone is a telephone you can take anywhere.
In Switzerland you dial 117 for the police, 118 for the fire brigade and 144 for an ambulance.
At payphones you paid with coins.
The International Telecommunication Union ITU in Geneva sets worldwide rules for telecommunications.

abschnitte.text: In the telephone's **microphone**, the voice makes a thin membrane vibrate. These vibrations are turned into electrical signals and passed on by cable or radio. At the receiving end, a small **loudspeaker** turns the signals back into sound. So you hear the voice even though the other person is far away.

Several inventors were working at the same time on the idea of transmitting speech electrically. The German **Philipp Reis** demonstrated a device that transmitted sounds as early as 1861. **Alexander Graham Bell**, who was born in Scotland, filed his patent in the USA in 1876 and is therefore usually regarded as the inventor of the telephone. Soon telephone networks were set up in many towns.

abschnitte.titel: From the switchboard operator to the mobile phone
abschnitte.text: At first, a telephone operator connected calls by hand using plugs at an **exchange**. Later, automatic systems took over this work, and people dialled the number with a rotary dial. On the street there were phone boxes with **payphones**, into which you put coins. From the 1990s the **mobile phone** spread, and since 2007 smartphones with touchscreens have been usual.

In an emergency the telephone can save lives. In Switzerland you dial **117** for the police, **118** for the fire brigade and **144** for an ambulance. The Europe-wide emergency number 112 also works. On the phone, say calmly who you are, where you are and what has happened.

For telephones all over the world to work together, shared rules are needed. They are drawn up by the **International Telecommunication Union** ITU, which has its headquarters in Geneva and is an organisation of the UN. Today many calls go over the internet or mobile networks instead of copper cables. With video calls you can even see each other while you talk.

begriffe.erklaerung: A legal right that reserves an invention for its inventor.
The place that used to connect telephone calls with each other.
A telephone number for help when you are in danger.
Making calls using radio waves and masts instead of cables.

gewusst: The first telephones had no numbers; you simply told the operator who you wanted to talk to.
Many old phone boxes in Switzerland have been turned into mini-libraries.
Bell wanted people to answer the phone with “Ahoy”.

teile.einleitung: A tunnel is an underground passage that leads through a mountain, under a river or under a city. Tunnels shorten journeys, protect against avalanches and connect valleys that would otherwise be separated by mountains. Switzerland is a land of tunnels: it is home to the Gotthard Base Tunnel, the longest railway tunnel in the world.
wichtigste: A tunnel is an artificially built underground route.
The longest railway tunnel in the world is the Gotthard Base Tunnel in Switzerland.
It opened in 2016 and is about 57 kilometres long.
Tunnels are blasted or dug with huge tunnel boring machines.
The first Gotthard railway tunnel opened in 1882.
Small tunnels are also built under roads for animals such as frogs and toads.
Moles and badgers are nature's tunnel builders.

abschnitte.text: A **tunnel** is an underground passage through which roads, railways, water or pipes and cables run. In mountainous countries such as Switzerland, tunnels connect valleys and make long, winding pass roads unnecessary. In cities, underground trains and other trains run through tunnels beneath the houses. Under the sea, tunnels even connect countries, for example the Channel Tunnel between England and France.

In hard rock, blasting is often used: holes are drilled, filled with **explosives**, and afterwards the rock is cleared away. For long tunnels, huge **tunnel boring machines** are used today, which eat their way through the mountain with a rotating cutting head. Then the tunnel is lined with concrete so that nothing collapses. Ventilation, lighting and emergency exits make it safe.

The **Gotthard Base Tunnel** between Erstfeld in the canton of Uri and Bodio in Ticino is the longest railway tunnel in the world, at about 57 kilometres. It opened in 2016 after 17 years of construction. Because it runs deep down in the mountain, trains hardly have to climb any more and can travel much faster. It is part of the **NRLA**, which also includes the Lötschberg Base Tunnel and the Ceneri Base Tunnel.

As early as 1882 the first **Gotthard railway tunnel** opened, about 15 kilometres long. Many workers died during its construction; most of them came from Italy. In 1980 came the Gotthard road tunnel for cars, almost 17 kilometres long. Today Switzerland has hundreds of railway and road tunnels.

Animals are tunnel builders too. The **mole** digs long passages with its shovel-like front paws and spends almost its whole life underground. The badger builds large setts with several entrances, sometimes more than ten. In Switzerland, small **amphibian tunnels** are built under some roads so that common frogs and common toads can travel safely to their spawning waters in spring.

begriffe.erklaerung: A huge machine that bores through rock with a rotating head.
New Railway Link through the Alps, the Swiss project for new Alpine tunnels.
A tunnel deep down at the foot of a mountain range.
A small tunnel under a road for frogs and toads.

gewusst: At its highest point, the rock above the Gotthard Base Tunnel is more than 2000 metres thick.
The miners from both sides met in the Gotthard Base Tunnel almost to the centimetre.
Saint Barbara is regarded as the patron saint of tunnel builders, which is why her figure often stands at the tunnel entrance.

teile.einleitung: A sailing ship is a ship driven by the wind. The wind blows into large pieces of cloth, the sails, and pushes the ship forward. For centuries, sailing ships were the fastest way to travel across the seas.
wichtigste: A sailing ship is driven by the wind.
The sails hang from masts and are adjusted with ropes.
Many explorers used caravels.
With clever technique, a sailing ship can even travel at an angle against the wind.
The Swiss team Alinghi won the America's Cup in 2003.
Today most people sail in their free time or as a sport.

abschnitte.text: A sailing ship has a **hull**, one or more **masts** and sails made of cloth. All the ropes and masts together are called the **rigging**. Under the hull, a keel stops the ship drifting sideways or capsizing. It is steered with the rudder at the stern.

If the wind comes from behind, the ship is simply pushed along. If it blows from the side, the sail works like a wing and pulls the ship forward. No sailing ship can sail directly into the wind. That is why it sails in a zigzag; this is called **tacking**.

In the 15th and 16th centuries, Portuguese and Spanish seafarers used **caravels**. These nimble ships could sail well even when the wind was unfavourable. In 1492, Christopher Columbus sailed to America with two caravels and one larger ship. Later the Dutch and the English built large merchant ships for the route to Asia.

In the 19th century the fast **clippers**, which brought tea from China to Europe, were famous. The “Cutty Sark” from 1869 can still be seen in London today. Huge cargo sailing ships were called windjammers. When steamships came along, the great sailing ships gradually disappeared.

People sail on many Swiss lakes, especially Lake Geneva, Lake Constance and Lake Zurich. Every year the **Bol d'Or** regatta takes place on Lake Geneva. The Geneva team **Alinghi**, owned by Ernesto Bertarelli, won the America's Cup in 2003 as the first European team and defended it in 2007. That was a sensation for a country without a sea.

begriffe.erklaerung: All the masts, sails and ropes of a sailing ship together.
Sailing in a zigzag against the wind.
A nimble sailing ship used by explorers in the 15th and 16th centuries.
A race between sailing boats.

gewusst: The America's Cup is one of the oldest sports trophies still contested in the world and dates from 1851.
Today some cargo ships are being fitted with large sails again to save fuel.

teile.einleitung: Hydropower is energy obtained from flowing or falling water. Centuries ago, water wheels were already driving mills; today hydropower stations produce electricity. In Switzerland, hydropower is the most important source of electricity.
wichtigste: Hydropower is a renewable energy source, like solar or wind power.
In a hydropower station, the water turns a turbine that drives a generator.
For more than a hundred years, Switzerland has obtained most of its electricity from hydropower.
Because it replaced the missing coal, hydropower was called “white coal”.
A pumped storage power station stores energy by pumping water uphill.
In 1769 Richard Arkwright invented the water frame, a spinning machine powered by water.
Hydropower helped Switzerland to industrialise early.

abschnitte.text: Water that flows downhill or falls from above has a lot of **kinetic energy**. This energy can be captured and used. In the past, **water wheels** drove mills, saws and hammer works. Today hydropower stations turn the power of water into electricity. Because the Sun keeps making water evaporate and fall again as rain, hydropower is **renewable**.

The water flows through pipes onto a **turbine** and makes it turn. The turbine is connected to a **generator**, which turns the rotation into electricity. The more water and the greater the drop, the more electricity is produced. Depending on the location, different turbines are used, such as the Pelton, Francis or Kaplan turbine. The electricity then flows through high-voltage lines to the consumers.

**Run-of-river power stations** are on rivers such as the Rhine and the Aare and supply electricity all the time. **Storage power stations** in the Alps hold back water in reservoirs behind high dams and release it when electricity is needed. **Pumped storage power stations** pump water up into an upper lake when there is surplus electricity. When electricity is needed later, it is let flow down again, so the power station works like a giant battery. Examples in Switzerland are Nant de Drance in Valais and Linth-Limmern in the canton of Glarus.

In the 18th century, in 1769, the Englishman Richard Arkwright invented the **water frame**, a spinning machine driven by water power. Because Switzerland has hardly any coal, many factories here were built on rivers and used water power. Together with the tradition of home working and exports, this helped Switzerland to **industrialise** early. Only the steam engine made factories elsewhere independent of water power. From about 1900, large power stations for producing electricity were built in Switzerland, and people spoke of **white coal**.

Thanks to the Alps, plenty of rain and glaciers, Switzerland has ideal conditions. There are about 700 larger hydropower stations here. They supply about 60 per cent of the country's own electricity (as of 2024). The highest dam is the **Grande Dixence** in Valais at 285 metres. One problem is that dams change rivers and block the way for fish, so **fish ladders** are built and care is taken to leave enough residual water.

begriffe.erklaerung: A wheel with blades that is turned by the water.
A machine that turns rotation into electric current.
A power station that stores energy by pumping water into a higher lake.
A stepped waterway that lets fish swim past a power station.

gewusst: The largest hydropower station in the world is the Three Gorges Dam on the Yangtze in China.
The caverns of the Nant de Drance pumped storage power station lie deep in the rock; the large machine hall is almost 200 metres long.
Even in ancient Rome, water wheels were used to grind grain.

teile.einleitung: A satellite is a spacecraft that circles the Earth in space on a fixed path. Satellites provide weather pictures, transmit television and phone calls and show us the way with navigation. The first artificial satellite, Sputnik 1, went into space in 1957.
wichtigste: An artificial satellite is a device that circles the Earth in an orbit.
The first artificial satellite was Sputnik 1 in 1957.
Geostationary satellites circle about 35,800 kilometres above the equator.
Navigation satellites such as those of Galileo help you find your own location.
In 2009 SwissCube was the first satellite built entirely in Switzerland.
The space mission CHEOPS is led by the University of Bern.
The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth.

abschnitte.text: A **satellite** is a celestial body or a device that circles a larger body. The Moon is a natural satellite of the Earth. Artificial satellites are taken into space by rockets. They do not fall down because they fly so fast that, because of the curve of the Earth, they keep falling past it.

On 4 October 1957, the Soviet Union launched **Sputnik 1**, the first artificial satellite, into space. It was a metal ball about 58 centimetres across and sent out a beeping radio signal. The USA was shocked, and so the space race between the two superpowers began. Only a few months later came the first American satellite, Explorer 1.

Many satellites fly a few hundred kilometres up; the International Space Station ISS is at about 400 kilometres. **Geostationary** satellites circle about 35,800 kilometres above the equator. They take exactly as long for one orbit as the Earth takes to turn once, so they seem to stand still in the sky. That is why satellite dishes for television can be pointed at them in a fixed position.

**Weather satellites** photograph clouds and help with weather forecasts. Communication satellites transmit television programmes, phone calls and the internet. Navigation satellites, such as those of the European system **Galileo**, help you find your exact location. Research satellites and space telescopes such as Hubble observe distant stars and galaxies.

In 2009 **SwissCube** was launched, a small cube-shaped satellite built by students at EPFL in Lausanne. The University of Bern leads the **CHEOPS** mission, which has been studying planets around other stars since 2019. The Swiss astronaut Claude Nicollier helped repair the Hubble Space Telescope in 1993 and 1999. Switzerland is a founding member of the European Space Agency ESA.

begriffe.erklaerung: The path on which a satellite circles the Earth.
A satellite that seems always to stay above the same point on Earth.
Old satellites and pieces of wreckage that circle the Earth uselessly.
A vehicle that carries satellites into space.

gewusst: Today several thousand active satellites circle the Earth, more than ever before.
At night you can see some satellites with the naked eye as moving points of light in the sky.
Sputnik 1 circled the Earth about every 96 minutes.

teile.einleitung: Hydrogen is the lightest and most common chemical element in the universe. In the periodic table it has the atomic number 1 and the symbol H. As an energy carrier, hydrogen could make lorries, trains and factories more climate-friendly in future.
wichtigste: In the periodic table, hydrogen has the atomic number 1.
Shortly after the Big Bang, mainly hydrogen and helium were formed.
The Sun shines because hydrogen fuses into helium inside it.
With electricity, water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen; this is called electrolysis.
A fuel cell turns the energy of hydrogen and oxygen directly into electricity.
Only water comes out of the exhaust of a fuel cell vehicle.
Hydrogen catches fire very easily and must be handled carefully.

abschnitte.text: Hydrogen is the simplest element; its atom consists of just one **proton** and one **electron**. It has the atomic number 1 and the chemical symbol H. At normal temperature, hydrogen is a colourless, odourless gas. It only becomes liquid at minus 253 degrees. Niels Bohr developed his **atomic model**, in which electrons circle the nucleus in fixed shells, using the hydrogen atom.

Shortly after the **Big Bang**, mainly hydrogen and helium were formed, hydrogen most of all. At that time helium made up about 25 per cent of the mass of normal matter, and almost all the rest was hydrogen. The first stars were also made mainly of these two gases. Our Sun shines because, inside it, hydrogen fuses into helium through **nuclear fusion**. Hydrogen is still the most common element in the universe today.

The English scientist Henry **Cavendish** described hydrogen as a separate substance in 1766. The Frenchman Antoine Lavoisier later gave it its name, which means “water maker”. This is because when hydrogen burns with oxygen, **water** is formed. On Earth, hydrogen hardly ever occurs on its own but is usually bound up, above all in water. All living things also contain a lot of hydrogen.

With electricity, water can be split into hydrogen and oxygen; this is called **electrolysis**. If the electricity comes from the sun, wind or water, it is called **green hydrogen**. In a **fuel cell**, hydrogen and oxygen combine again, producing electricity and water. A fuel cell vehicle therefore gives off only water from its exhaust. In Switzerland, lorries have been running on hydrogen since 2020, among others for retailers.

Hydrogen catches fire very easily and can form an explosive mixture with air. In 1937 the hydrogen-filled airship **Hindenburg** went up in flames in the USA. Today strict safety rules apply to tanks and filling stations. One problem is that a lot of energy is lost when hydrogen is produced. In addition, most hydrogen is still made from natural gas; it is called **grey hydrogen**.

begriffe.erklaerung: Splitting water into hydrogen and oxygen with the help of electricity.
A device that produces electricity directly from hydrogen and oxygen.
The joining of light atomic nuclei, which releases a great deal of energy.
The number of an element in the periodic table; it shows the number of protons in the nucleus.

gewusst: A balloon filled with hydrogen rises even faster than one filled with helium.
About two thirds of all the atoms in your body are hydrogen atoms.
Every second, the Sun turns hundreds of millions of tonnes of hydrogen into helium.

teile.einleitung: An order says what comes first, what comes next and what comes at the end.
